The '''Bihari–LaSalle inequality''' was proved by the American mathematician
[[Joseph P. LaSalle]] (1916–1983) in 1949<ref>{{cite journal | title = Uniqueness theorems and successive approximations | author = J. LaSalle | journal =Annals of Mathematics |date=July 1949 | volume = 50 | number = 3  | pages = 722–730 | doi = 10.2307/1969559| jstor = 1969559 }}</ref> and by the Hungarian mathematician
Imre Bihari (1915–1998) in 1956.<ref>{{cite journal | title = A generalization of a lemma of Bellman and its application to uniqueness problems of differential equations | author = I. Bihari | journal = [[Acta Mathematica Hungarica]] |date=March 1956 | volume = 7 | number = 1  | pages = 81–94 | doi = 10.1007/BF02022967 | doi-access = free | hdl = 10338.dmlcz/101943 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> It is the following nonlinear generalization of [[Grönwall's lemma]].

Let ''u'' and ''&fnof;'' be non-negative [[continuous function]]s defined on the half-infinite [[ray (mathematics)|ray]] [0,&nbsp;∞), and let ''w'' be a continuous [[non-decreasing function]] defined on [0,&nbsp;∞) and ''w''(''u'')&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 on (0,&nbsp;∞). If ''u'' satisfies the following [[integral]] [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]],

: <math>u(t)\leq \alpha+ \int_0^t f(s)\,w(u(s))\,ds,\qquad t\in[0,\infty),</math>

where <math>\alpha</math> is a non-negative [[constant (mathematics)|constant]], then

: <math>u(t)\leq G^{-1}\left(G(\alpha)+\int_0^t\,f(s) \, ds\right),\qquad t\in[0,T],</math>

where the function ''G'' is defined by

: <math>G(x)=\int_{x_0}^x \frac{dy}{w(y)},\qquad x \geq 0,\,x_0>0, </math>

and ''G''<sup>−1</sup> is the [[inverse function]] of ''G'' and ''T'' is chosen so that

: <math>G(\alpha)+\int_0^t\,f(s)\,ds\in \operatorname{Dom}(G^{-1}),\qquad \forall \, t \in [0,T].</math>
